title: We built a non-LLM quant investment platform that scores its own predictions every trading day
author: MehmetSaruhan
selftext:
Hello

I know Reddit is currently flooded with “AI wrappers” that simply plug stock prices into ChatGPT or Claude and call it a day. As an independent developer with over 20 years of experience in strategy, forecasting, and quantitative engineering, I wanted to build something that’s truly grounded in financial mathematics rather than just text completion.

It’s called Opulence Alpha ([https://opulencealpha.ai/](https://opulencealpha.ai/)).

The Problem I’m Trying to Solve

Individual investors are often stuck between two bad options: paying high management fees for broad passive funds or trading based on news noise and gut instinct. On the other hand:

Elite financial advisory services remain locked behind high net worth thresholds due to manual operational costs.

The best quantitative infrastructure (such as Renaissance, Two Sigma, or Citadel) operates entirely behind closed doors.

How I Developed It

Instead of wrapping an LLM, I developed an independent quantitative engine trained on over 45 years of market history, tracking 1,979 daily data points per company and 14 independent risk engines.

The system operates in a continuous 3-step cycle:

1. Forecasts: Generates multi-horizon forecasts with explicit statistical uncertainty (conformal quantile regression + gradient-boosted trees).
2. Recommends: An Agentic Portfolio Manager translates these forecasts into actionable decisions (buy, hold, reduce, sell, rebalance) within strict risk limits.
3. Adapts: On each trading day, the platform compares its past forecasts and recommendations with actual market outcomes, scores them, and applies evolutionary reweighting to its models.

What Doesn’t It Do?

Does the 3-step cycle (Forecast → Recommend → Adapt) make sense to you, or does it seem too complex?

What research features or risk metrics would prevent you from using a tool like this for your own portfolio?

What’s confusing or incorrect on the site?

Feel free to critique the user interface, question the architecture, or test the platform at opulencealpha.ai. I’ll be in the comments to answer any technical or business-related questions!

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body:
The Forecast → Recommend → Adapt cycle makes sense, but how does daily evolutionary reweighting handle forecasts whose horizons haven't elapsed? A one-month forecast issued yesterday doesn't yet have a realized one-month outcome to score.

For the conformal quantile regression, I'd want a coverage report by forecast horizon, showing the fraction of outcomes inside the originally published intervals alongside interval widths. Keep those original forecasts attributable to the model version that issued them, even after weights change. That would make the image's “What survives testing?” concrete and help reveal whether adaptation preserves calibration or just widens intervals.

replies.author: MehmetSaruhan
replies.body:
That’s already accounted for in our architecture.

We have **300+ trading days of prediction history** for both Conformal Quantile Regression and the BOA layer, across multiple forecast horizons. A forecast is not scored until its corresponding horizon has actually elapsed, so a 21-day or 63-day forecast issued yesterday simply remains **pending**, rather than being prematurely reweighted.

Every prediction is also persisted with its **original model/version, issue date, horizon, published quantiles and interval**, so subsequent BOA weight changes do not alter the historical forecast that was actually issued.

As outcomes mature, we score them against the original forecast and feed the realized evidence into the evolutionary reweighting process. For Conformal, this lets us measure **coverage and interval width by horizon and model/version**, rather than simply looking at aggregate performance.

So the distinction is:

**Issued → Pending → Matured → Scored → Reweighted**

That historical attribution is essential; otherwise adaptation could contaminate the evidence it is supposed to learn from.

you can check out  [https://opulencealpha.ai/faq](https://opulencealpha.ai/faq) for more answer... Or we tested 24 popular beliefs repeated on every trading forum [https://opulencealpha.ai/studies](https://opulencealpha.ai/studies)

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body:
The Forecast → Recommend → Adapt loop makes sense conceptually — it's basically an online-learning quant pipeline with a human-readable decision layer on top, which is a reasonable architecture. Where I'd push for more specificity, since you asked what would stop someone from trusting it with real capital: the "45 years of market history" and "1,979 daily data points per company" numbers sound impressive but are meaningless without knowing what the actual out-of-sample track record looks like — conformal quantile regression is good specifically because it gives calibrated uncertainty bounds, so the natural question is whether you're publishing calibration plots (are your 80% intervals actually covering \~80% of realized outcomes out of sample?), not just point-forecast accuracy. That's the number serious quant shops actually scrutinize, and it's usually the first thing that's missing from "we built a quant platform" posts.

The "evolutionary reweighting" step is also the part I'd want more detail on before trusting it — adapting model weights daily based on how recent forecasts scored is exactly the kind of mechanism that can quietly overfit to recent regime noise if there's no explicit regularization or lookback-window discipline built in, so worth being upfront on-site about how you're guarding against that. On the UI side, the biggest thing that'd build trust fast is a live or paper-traded performance page updating in real time against the model's own published forecasts, rather than backtested stats — self-reported live-forward numbers are worth far more than backtest metrics at this stage, which is honestly the same standard I'd hold EventTrader's own signal work to. [https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH](https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH)

replies.author: MehmetSaruhan
replies.body:
Fair points. I agree that 45 years of history and 1,979 daily features are infrastructure numbers, not evidence of predictive performance by themselves.

On the calibration point, we have **300+ trading days of realized prediction history** for the Conformal Quantile Regression layer. Forecasts remain attributable to the model/version and timestamp that produced them, and a forecast is only scored once its horizon has matured. So an 80% interval can be evaluated against its actual out-of-sample coverage rather than retrospectively recalculated after adaptation.

The same principle applies to  Bernstein Online Aggregation (BOA)/evolutionary reweighting: we don't score an immature forecast, and changing weights doesn't rewrite the historical forecast that was issued. The point of the evaluation layer is precisely to measure whether adaptation improves realized outcomes rather than simply fitting recent noise.

And I agree on the last point: **forward, timestamped evidence is much more meaningful than a static backtest.** That's why we're building the platform around continuously measured predictions, outcomes and portfolio decisions rather than presenting one backtest as proof of alpha.

One distinction I'd make, though: we're not positioning the system as “60% accuracy = 60% probability of making money.” A forecast is evidence. The portfolio layer has to determine whether that evidence actually changes a decision after uncertainty, regime, concentration, risk constraints and transaction costs.

That's ultimately what we're trying to measure: **not whether the model can predict, but whether the prediction survives testing and improves the portfolio decision.**

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
The version-locked, score-only-after-maturity design is exactly the right architecture — that's the part that actually prevents the retroactive-recalculation problem most "adaptive" systems quietly have, so credit where due.

The remaining gap is just visibility, not methodology: with 300+ days of scored history, is the actual coverage number published anywhere — i.e., "our 80% intervals covered X% of realized outcomes over this period"? That's a single chart, and it's the thing that would move this from "we built the right evaluation architecture" to "here's proof it's working," which is a meaningfully stronger claim than describing the methodology alone.

The distinction you're drawing at the end — forecast evidence vs. portfolio decision — is the right one, and it raises the natural next question: do you separately publish realized portfolio-level return/Sharpe net of transaction costs, distinct from forecast calibration? A well-calibrated forecast doesn't automatically survive the risk-constraint and cost layer intact, and that's usually where the gap between "good model" and "good outcome" actually shows up. If both numbers are tracked and timestamped the way the forecasts are, publishing them side by side would be a strong differentiator from the usual "AI quant platform" post.

replies.author: MehmetSaruhan
replies.body:
Yes — and there are additional safeguards beyond simply using recent realized returns.

Each forecast horizon has its own **forgetting mechanism through Bernstein Online Aggregation (BOA)**, so the system isn't simply chasing the latest regime with one global weighting scheme. We also use multiple model families specifically to avoid relying on a single modeling approach.

More importantly, the adaptive layer sits within **five intelligence services**. The Experience layer continuously generates hypotheses about model behaviour, regime patterns and other persistent effects. When a hypothesis survives testing, the relevant intelligence service incorporates it into its subsequent decision process.

So adaptation isn't driven only by realized returns or BOA weights. There are multiple layers of evidence, validation and safeguards around it.

We're documenting these mechanisms, including the calibration and portfolio-level evaluation, and plan to publish the details in a technical article with the team later this year.

By the way you can visit our currently published studies: [https://opulencealpha.ai/studies](https://opulencealpha.ai/studies)
